ICLR 2025Memory for scientific reasoning

ChemAgent: Self-updating Library in Large Language Models Improves Chemical Reasoning

Xiangru Tang, Tianyu Hu, Muyang Ye, Yanjun Shao, Xunjian Yin, Siru Ouyang, Wangchunshu Zhou, Pan Lu, Zhuosheng Zhang, Yilun Zhao, Arman Cohan, Mark Gerstein

Paper ↗arXiv ↗Code ↗

ChemAgent turns solved chemistry subproblems into reusable memory, helping an LLM plan, calculate, and refine new solutions with experience retained outside its model weights.

01 / The research question

Reuse the part of a solution that transfers

Two chemistry questions may share a calculation even when their complete solutions look different. Retrieving an entire worked example can bury that useful operation under irrelevant conditions. ChemAgent stores smaller units: the conditions under which a subproblem is posed, the subproblem itself, and its solution. This representation makes prior work available at the point where the new calculation needs it.

A library does not remove every failure mode. The paper’s error analysis (Figure 7) examines an entropy problem for a gas compressed reversibly and adiabatically, a process with no entropy change. The agent’s plan ignores that condition and applies ΔS = n·C_V,m·ln(T_final/T_initial), while the memories it retrieves, about standard reaction entropy and the temperature dependence of cell potentials, are irrelevant to an adiabatic process. A flawed decomposition and irrelevant retrieval compound each other, so the quality of the plan matters as much as the contents of the library.

02 / Inside the method

Memory must support both execution and replanning

The initial library is built from development problems with supplied solutions. Their conditions are extracted and checked, their solutions are decomposed, and low-confidence memory units are filtered. Planning memory retains higher-level strategies; execution memory stores the structured subproblems. Knowledge memory is different: formulas and principles are generated for the current problem and are not permanently added to the shared library.

Consider the electron-wavelength example in the framework figure. Given a kinetic energy of 100 eV, the task is decomposed into two sub-tasks: use the kinetic-energy formula to obtain the electron’s velocity, then use the de Broglie formula to compute its wavelength. Each sub-task retrieves its own memories, so a previous velocity calculation can help without requiring the entire earlier question to match. The result of one sub-task becomes a condition for the next.

Review can change either the current answer or the remaining plan. A unit error calls for revising a sub-solution. A subtask that calculates energy when wavelength is requested requires restructuring subsequent steps. This distinction matters: repeatedly correcting arithmetic cannot rescue a plan aimed at the wrong quantity. If no suitable execution memory exists, the agent can construct related practice problems from its own knowledge.

  1. 01

    Build reusable memory

    Decompose worked problems into planning strategies and structured subproblem solutions.

  2. 02

    Retrieve and solve

    Retrieve related experiences and generate task-specific chemistry knowledge to guide each subproblem.

  3. 03

    Refine and retain

    Evaluate intermediate solutions, revise the plan when needed, and add new experiences to the library.

03 / Reading the evidence

Separate a growing library from guaranteed improvement

  • 57.16%

    Average accuracy · GPT-4

    Across four SciBench chemistry datasets, ChemAgent exceeds the 47.66% average reported for StructChem under the paper's setup.

  • 52.12%

    Without evaluation and refinement

    Removing solution review lowers average accuracy from 57.16%, showing that memory and active correction contribute together.

The GPT-4 ablation in Table 1 separates the contributions: removing evaluation and refinement lowers the reported average by 5.04 percentage points, and removing memory as well lowers it by another 2.90 points. Thus the full gain cannot be attributed to storing examples alone. Review adds computation: the paper reports roughly 12,000 tokens per problem without review and 23,000 with it, excluding initial library construction.

The repeated-exposure experiment is narrower than unrestricted autonomous learning. It uses MATTER, removes the review module, retains experiences judged correct, and excludes a problem’s own earlier memory when solving that problem again. These controls help isolate reuse across problems. They also make correctness feedback and memory quality part of the result; a larger unfiltered library is not automatically a better one.

Research summary

Chemical reasoning usually involves complex, multi-step processes that demand precise calculations, where even minor errors can lead to cascading failures. Furthermore, large language models (LLMs) encounter difficulties handling domain-specific formulas, executing reasoning steps accurately, and integrating code effectively when tackling chemical reasoning tasks. To address these challenges, we present ChemAgent, a novel framework designed to improve the performance of LLMs through a dynamic, self-updating library. This library is developed by decomposing chemical tasks into sub-tasks and compiling these sub-tasks into a structured collection that can be referenced for future queries. Then, when presented with a new problem, ChemAgent retrieves and refines pertinent information from the library, which we call memory, facilitating effective task decomposition and the generation of solutions. Our method designs three types of memory and a library-enhanced reasoning component, enabling LLMs to improve over time through experience. Experimental results on four chemical reasoning datasets from SciBench demonstrate that ChemAgent achieves performance gains of up to 46% (GPT-4), significantly outperforming existing methods. Our findings suggest substantial potential for future applications, including tasks such as drug discovery and materials science.
